'''''Eragrostis curvula''''' is a species of [[Poaceae|grass]] known by the [[common name]] '''weeping lovegrass'''. Other common names include '''Boer lovegrass''', '''curved lovegrass''', '''Catalina lovegrass''', and '''African lovegrass'''.

It is native to [[southern Africa]]. It is an [[introduced species]] on other continents.<ref name=feis>Gucker, Corey L. (2009). [http://www.fs.fed.us/database/feis/plants/graminoid/eracur/all.html ''Eragrostis curvula''.] In: Fire Effects Information System, [Online]. U.S. Department of Agriculture, Forest Service, Rocky Mountain Research Station, Fire Sciences Laboratory. Retrieved 12-22-2011.</ref>

==Description==
''Eragrostis curvula'' is usually a long-lived perennial grass, but it is sometimes an [[annual plant]]. It is variable in appearance, and there are many different natural and cultivated forms.

In general, it forms tufts of stems up to {{convert|1.9|m|ft}} tall. The tufts may reach a diameter of {{convert|38|cm|ft}}.

The grass grows from a thick root network. Plants have been noted to have roots penetrating over {{convert|4|m|ft}} deep in the soil and {{convert|3|m|ft}} laterally. The roots can grow {{convert|5|cm|in}} per day. The first root to grow into the soil from a [[seedling]] can send out up to 60 small rootlets per inch. The dense root system forms a [[sod]].

The drooping leaves of the grass are up to {{convert|65|cm|ft}} long but just a few millimeters wide, and they may have rolled edges. The [[inflorescence]] is a [[panicle]] with branches lined with centimeter-long spikelets. Each spikelet may contain up to 15 flowers. One panicle may produce 1000 seeds. Cultivated plants may produce two crops of seed per year. The plant self-fertilizes or undergoes [[apomixis]], without fertilization.<ref name=feis/>

==Uses==
This grass is valuable as a [[forage]] for livestock in Africa, its native range.<ref name=ncan>Ncanana, S., et al. (2005). [https://doi.org/10.1007%2Fs00299-005-0940-1 Development of plant regeneration and transformation protocols for the desiccation-sensitive weeping lovegrass ''Eragrostis curvula''.] ''Plant Cell Rep'' '''24''' 335-40. Retrieved 12-22-2011.</ref> There are many [[ecotype]]s. Several of these ecotypes were collected and introduced in the United States as [[cultivar]]s. The grass was first planted in the United States in [[Stillwater, Oklahoma]], in 1935. It was good for livestock, and its massive root network made it a good plant for [[erosion]] control.

It spread quickly as it was planted for [[ornamental plant|ornamental]] purposes. It reached [[New York (state)|New York]] in the 1960s and in the 1970s and 80s it was planted alongside many highways such as the [[Long Island Expressway]]. Today it occurs as an [[invasive species]] in wild habitat from the southwestern United States to the [[East Coast of the United States|East Coast]]. It can be found in woodlands, [[chaparral]], [[prairie]], [[grassland]], and disturbed areas.<ref name=feis/> It is tolerant of very acidic and very basic soils; it grows easily in [[mining|mine spoils]]. This species may [[Hybrid (biology)|hybridize]] with other ''[[Eragrostis]]'', such as ''[[Eragrostis caesia]]'', ''[[Eragrostis lehmanniana|E. lehmanniana]]'', and ''[[Eragrostis planiculmis|E. planiculmis]]''.<ref name=az>Halvorson, W. L. and P. Guertin. (2003). [http://sdrsnet.srnr.arizona.edu/data/sdrs/ww/docs/eragcurv.pdf USGS Weeds in the West project: Status of Introduced Plants in Southern Arizona Parks.] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120426065232/http://sdrsnet.srnr.arizona.edu/data/sdrs/ww/docs/eragcurv.pdf |date=2012-04-26 }} USGS. Retrieved 12-22-2011.</ref>

Cultivars of this grass include 'South African Robusta Blue', 'Witbank', 'Ermelo', 'Kromdraai', 'American Leafy', and 'Renner'.<ref name=Maple>'Mapledoram, B. and E. P. Theron. (1970). ''Notes on the relative merit of four cultivars of ''Eragrostis curvula'' in Natal''. Proceedings of the Annual Congresses of the Grassland Society of Southern Africa</ref> Cultivars may be selected for yield, palatability for livestock, and [[drought tolerance|drought resistance]]. It is planted along waterways in [[Sri Lanka]] and mountainsides in [[Japan]], and it is used for oversowing fields in [[Argentina]]. In the United States it is often planted alongside [[Kummerowia stipulacea|Korean lespedeza]].<ref name=fao>[http://www.fao.org/ag/AGP/agpc/doc/gbase/Safricadata/eragcur.htm ''Eragrostis curvula''.] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20121020100721/http://www.fao.org/ag/agp/AGPC/doc/Gbase/Safricadata/eragcur.htm |date=2012-10-20 }} FAO Plant Profile. Retrieved 12-22-2011.</ref> It is planted as a [[nurse crop]] for [[Lespedeza cuneata|sericea lespedeza]], [[Panicum amarum|coastal panic grass]], and [[Panicum virgatum|switchgrass]].<ref name=fs />

It is an [[invasive species]] in some regions, such as parts of the United States and [[Victoria, Australia|Victoria]] and other Australian states.<ref name=pars>Parsons, W. T. and E. G. Cuthbertson. ''Noxious weeds of Australia''. CSIRO Publishing 2001.
</ref> It is aggressive and can crowd out native plants. Its drought resistance helps it to survive in dry environments.<ref name=az/><ref name=fs>[https://plants.sc.egov.usda.gov/DocumentLibrary/factsheet/pdf/fs_ercu2.pdf ''Eragrostis curvula''.] USFS Plant Fact Sheet. Retrieved 7-20-2021.</ref>

In [[Lesotho]], this grass is used to make baskets, brooms, hats, ropes, and candles, and it is used for food, as a charm, and in funeral rituals.<ref name=purd>[http://www.hort.purdue.edu/newcrop/duke_energy/Eragrostis_curvula.html ''Eragrostis curvula''.] Purdue University Center for New Crops and Plants Products. Retrieved 12-22-2011.</ref>
